ledger.sentence: The NHS says a colonoscopy is often done to find the cause of bowel symptoms.
Other reasons include looking for early signs of bowel cancer in people at high risk, and checking after earlier treatment for bowel cancer.
People who have had polyps removed before, or who have a family history of bowel cancer, may also be referred.
For a clear view, the bowel needs to be empty.
Trusts generally prescribe a laxative solution, often a powder mixed with water, to empty the bowel.
One trust describes the preparation as taking laxatives, cutting down on fibre, and stopping all food in the last few hours beforehand.
Leaflets warn of frequent diarrhoea, cramping and nausea, and advise staying near a toilet.
One trust notes that the laxative can cause dehydration, light-headedness, low blood pressure or kidney problems.
Preparation details differ between trusts, and the hospital sends its own instructions.
ledger.note: Summary differences (low fibre diet 3 days at some).

ledger.sentence: A nurse sees the person first to discuss their medical history, carry out simple checks and explain what will happen.
A thin, flexible tube with a camera is passed through the anus and around the large bowel.
Air is pumped in to open the bowel, which can cause bloating or cramps.
The NHS says a colonoscopy can be uncomfortable but should not be painful.
The procedure itself takes about 30 to 45 minutes, and a person may be at the hospital for about two hours in total.
ledger.note: NHS 30-45 min; two hours at hospital.

ledger.sentence: A leaflet says some people have sedation, some breathe a pain-relieving gas called Entonox, and some have no pain relief.
ledger.note: Summary: sedation, Entonox or no anaesthetic.

ledger.sentence: Sedation is given through a small needle in the back of the hand.
Polyps are growths on the bowel lining, and they are usually not cancer.
It is not possible to tell by looking whether a polyp contains cancer cells, so polyps are removed and examined under a microscope.
Staff can also take small tissue samples, called biopsies, which is painless.
Afterwards the person is usually told whether any polyps were removed or samples taken.
The NHS describes colonoscopy as a common and straightforward procedure.
The main risks are a tear in the bowel wall, called perforation, and bleeding.
Trust leaflets give perforation figures that differ, and one says it happens to about one person in 1,000 nationally.
ledger.note: Summary: 1 in 2511 vs about 1 in 1000. Number conditional.

ledger.sentence: The risk rises when polyps are removed, especially large or complex ones.
Sometimes a hole can be closed with clips during the procedure.
It is common to pass a small amount of blood from the anus after a biopsy or polyp removal.
Colonoscopy is very accurate, but occasionally a problem, including rarely a cancer, can be missed.
Severe belly pain, heavy bleeding or a fever after the test needs urgent help: NHS 111 or the hospital unit, and 999 if it is severe.
A letter or call with the results usually comes two to three weeks after a colonoscopy.
A normal result means no polyps or cancer were found in the bowel.
If a biopsy was taken, the biopsy results can take up to two weeks.
A colonoscopy passes a thin, flexible tube with a camera through the bowel to look for the cause of symptoms, to screen for bowel cancer, or to follow up earlier problems.
ledger.note: NHS why it's done; trust leaflet.

ledger.sentence: The bowel must be empty for a clear view, so a laxative preparation is taken beforehand and often causes frequent diarrhoea.
Polyps, which are growths on the bowel lining, can be removed during the test and examined under a microscope.
Perforation, a tear in the bowel wall, is the main serious risk and is uncommon, with higher risk when polyps are removed.
A colonoscopy uses a thin camera to look inside the large bowel. This guide covers bowel preparation, sedation, risks and when results arrive.
ledger.note: Summary restates the supported sentences below.
